title: Performance in good faith: editorial notes and questions
summary: Read the surrounding notes and questions alongside the principal cases. The complete assigned pages are preserved here.
notes:
Dalton v. Educational Testing Service: Dalton is the clearest worked example of contractual discretion in this course: identify who has the choice, what process was promised, what facts bear on that choice, and how a remedy can enforce the process without dictating the result.

Northwest, Inc. v. Ginsberg: Read this after Dalton to see why the source of an obligation matters. A court must identify the governing state rule and any controlling federal statute before applying a general account of good faith.

Market Street Associates v. Frey: Market Street explains good faith through a particular misuse of an existing contractual mechanism. It also shows why a case’s procedural stage matters when its outcome depends on a person’s knowledge.

Bloor v. Falstaff Brewing Corp.: Bloor explains how a flexible business obligation can still be enforceable. It identifies the promised objective, considers the promisor’s financial capacity, examines concrete decisions, and gives a workable damages method.

Ng Giap Hon v. Westcomb Securities Pte Ltd and Others: Ng Giap belongs beside Dalton and Market Street as a jurisdiction-specific counterpoint. It also explains why the source and specificity of a proposed limit on discretion matter.
